note.text:
This video will shock you.
I will probably never believe the story if not that it was captured on video.

24years ago, during the Big Brother Brasil 2, there was a contestant called Cida Moraes. On one of the days, she was sunbathing alone outside of the house. 

Then she suddenly heard a voice from nowhere calling her name (“Cida? Cida?”). She looked around and saw nobody. The voice sounded like her sister. But her sister was not, and is not inside Big Brother house. And no one else heard it. But she was sure she heard her sister call her voice.

What Cida did not know was that her sister, Gloria, had died that same moment from breast cancer. Gloria had breast cancer before Cida went into the game show.

Because Cida was in Big Brother House, she was already cut off from the outside world so she never knew her sister had become very ill and was in the hospital intensive care unit before she later died.

The game show crew informed her later that same day that her sister died earlier in the day around the same time she heard her sister’s voice -that nobody else heard. It was almost as if someone nobody else could see or hear came to inform her that her sister had died. Or maybe the sister came herself. 

Otherwise how do you explain that someone locked out in a game show from the outside world will suddenly hear her sister call her voice the very moment she died? A voice nobody else heard? A sister she didn’t even know had become severely ill?

We would never know the answers. But Cida’s reaction was all captured on this video. 

There is far more to this world than the physical. Pls don’t live your life thinking all there is to this world is just what your eyes can see, and your hands can touch.

A politician who is about to wield influence in Washington is always subject to scrutiny.

Abdul El-Sayed’s rise to the US Senate has Michigan talking, but his Indian connection at home is interesting. Very interesting. 

Bhatkal is a name Indians remember from some of the darkest years of Islamist terrorism in this country. 

His wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, traces her family roots to Bhatkal in Karnataka - a town whose name became notorious for the formation of the Islamic terrorist group - the Indian Mujahideen - that carried out multiple terror attacks in India. The terror group’s leadership included brothers Riyaz and Iqbal Bhatkal along with Yasin Bhatkal masterminding major serial bomb blasts across the country.

His father-in-law, Dr Tayeb Jukaku, served on the founders’ committee of the Islamic Society of North America and held leadership positions at CAIR Michigan. Both organisations were named as unindicted co-conspirators in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing case.

El-Sayed’s own record raises questions that deserve answers and they begin in Egypt.

In 2012, he signed a statement supporting then-President of Egypt Mohamed Morsi, a Muslim Brotherhood leader, and backing his controversial decree shielding presidential decisions from judicial review. The statement also called for the media and police to be purged.

A year earlier, El-Sayed had written that fears of a Muslim Brotherhood takeover should not deter American support for Egypt’s pro-democracy protests.

Then there are the 2012 posts by his half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi. She wrote that her family had long been associated with the Muslim Brotherhood and referred to their mother’s activism in the organisation in the 1970s.

So, the American leftist media can celebrate a historic victory all it likes. But a historic victory does not make a politician’s past and present disappear.
